fields.meta_description: Build a pulse survey that charts each group against its own past scores and alerts a manager when a score drops. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Pulse Survey That Tracks the Trend Round by Round
fields.hero_description: Describe who answers and how often. Emergent builds the short question set, the schedule, a trend line per team and the alert when a line turns, in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Keeps a Pulse Survey Useful
fields.features_subheading: A pulse survey repeats a short set of questions on a fixed schedule to show how answers move between rounds.
fields.feature_1:
Core items that never change

Locks the same core statements into every cycle, word for word, which lets a March score sit cleanly beside June's. Rotating items come and go with one message to Emergent.
fields.feature_2:
A cadence you set per group

Sends weekly or every other week, on the day and hour you pick. Reminders reach only the people who have not answered yet, and each round closes on schedule regardless.
fields.feature_3:
A trend line for every team

Charts each team cycle by cycle against its own average instead of the company's. A real slide shows up within two rounds, while a one-week dip stays small on the chart.
fields.feature_4:
Group minimums for confidentiality

Hides any team or comment set with fewer answers than the minimum you choose, such as five. Results open once a group crosses that line, and no view ever shows a name.
fields.feature_5:
Questions where people already are

Posts each question as a Slack message or an email. Staff without a work account scan a QR code in the break room instead, and every answer lands in the same response table.
fields.feature_6:
Your pulse app, in your GitHub

Exports the finished app to your GitHub on paid plans, including the questions, schedule logic, dashboards and response database. Host it yourself or keep building it in Emergent.

fields.tab_content_1:
Payments dips under a six-cycle average

Every other Monday, 220 people in a product org answer six questions about workload and manager support. Each team is charted against its own six-cycle average, not the company's. When Payments fell to 3.4, 0.6 under its average, the team's manager got a Slack message naming the lowest item.
fields.tab_content_2:
Ratings come in through Slack on Mondays

Remote staff get a pulse question as a Slack message each Monday morning and rate it 1 to 5 without opening another app. Questions rotate through a bank of 12 items, and each returns every 12 weeks with its own trend. A team's result stays hidden until five answers are in, and every rating is saved with its team tag.
fields.tab_content_3:
Which office the new schedule is failing

After a switch to a new hybrid schedule, staff at four offices answer a short pulse each Friday. The item that matters is the statement "The new schedule works for me." When agreement at any office falls below 60%, that office's lead gets an email with the week's comments. Denver tripped it this week.
fields.tab_content_4:
Key accounts rate the service monthly

Once a month, 40 key accounts get two questions by email: a service score out of 10 and an open box for what to fix. Each score sits beside last month's. A drop of 2 points or more puts the account on its manager's list with the comment attached. Initech landed there this month after a 3-point drop.

fields.howto_title: How to Run a Pulse Survey
fields.howto_description: A pulse proves its worth over many rounds, not one. Keep it short enough that people answer the tenth round as readily as the first.
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Set the cadence and the minimum
fields.howto_step_1_des: Start with the one decision the pulse should inform, such as whether a new on-call rotation is wearing a team down. Without one, the questions drift and the results have no audience. Write that decision at the top of the brief.
fields.howto_step_2_des: The more often a pulse runs, the shorter it should be. Five statements on a 1-5 agreement scale suit a weekly or biweekly round. Freeze their wording once the first round goes out, or the trend line compares two different questions.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Choose the day, the hour and how long each round stays open. Then set the smallest group that may see its own results. Below that number, answers still count toward the company figure but never show for the group on its own.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Write it out in plain English: who answers, which statements, the scale, the channel and the alert rule. Emergent builds a working pulse with its own response table and team dashboards. A later change, such as a new rotating item, takes one more message.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Say what happens to the answers
fields.howto_step_5_des: Open the first round with two plain facts: who sees results, and how small a group can be before its results hide. People answer a recurring survey honestly only when they trust those two facts, and the trust has to last for months.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Read the line, not the dot
fields.howto_step_6_des: A single low round can be a bad week. Two in a row against the team's own average is a signal worth a conversation. Compare each team with its own past, not with other teams whose work and pressures differ.
fields.howto_step_7_des: After a drop, the manager tells the team what they heard and the one change they will try. The next rounds show whether it worked. A pulse that changes nothing gives people no reason to keep answering.
